newsitem.title: USA: Russia-IMF 97 deal sets tough tax, revenue targets.
newsitem.headline: Russia-IMF 97 deal sets tough tax, revenue targets.

text.p: Russia's 1997 agreement with the International Monetary Fund will force Moscow to meet ambitious targets on revenue collection and structural reforms, an international monetary official said on Tuesday.
The official told Reuters that Russia could face serious problems if the targets were not met.
"The 1997 program is very ambitious on the revenue side and even if they achieve that the expenditures they can finance are very low. But that is the only way they can survive," he said.
"If they fail on the revenue side and cannot finance these expenditures, then they are really in very deep trouble, politically and socially. They will not be able to pay wages and pensions."

Wage and pension arrears are already a major problem for the Russian government, which is drawing up plans for drastic spending cuts to bring a stalled $10 billion, three-year IMF loan program back on track.

The loan is divided into three annual tranches and a source with Russia's IMF delegation said Central Bank chairman Sergei Dubinin signed an agreement on 1997 policy on Tuesday and Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin would sign soon.
"It sets fiscal targets for revenues and the deficit on a quarterly basis," the Russian source said, adding: "I'm not authorized to give you the figures."
The international monetary official said Russia still had to approve some regulations on issues like privatization before the IMF could recommend the 1997 program to its executive board.
He described revenue and structural issues as the key elements of the new document.
On the structural front, Russia had to curb the rising power of non-market oriented sectors which have grown more powerful over the five years since Russia launched its economic reforms.
"If they were to be allowed to get stronger still, it would be very difficult to dislodge them and the economy would be totally dominated by those interests," he said.
Other issues to be addressed included land privatization and efforts to make accountancy more transparent, he said.
He said the IMF was less worried about Moscow's ability to meet monetary targets contained in the document.
"They have shown over the last two years that they have handled monetary policy well and we are confident that this will be okay," he said.
Russian annual inflation fell to 21.8 percent last year, from 131 percent in 1995 and the Russian source said that the 1997 deal targetted 1997 inflation of 12 percent.
The IMF delayed several monthly disbursements of its Russia loan this year because it was worried about low tax revenues.
But officials have said they expect to disburse the first of a new series of quarterly tranches next months.
Deputies in both houses of parliament have served notice that they will oppose the government's plan to cut spending.
But parliamentary approval of a new budget will not be a condition of the 1997 IMF agreement.
